prompt: Which fraction is closest to 2?

solutions.title: Rewrite the fractions
solutions.body:
Each fraction has the form $\frac{n+10}{n}=1+\frac{10}{n}$ with $n=19,29,39,49,59$. All lie between $1$ and $2$, so the closest to $2$ is the largest, which has the smallest $n$: $\frac{29}{19}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{29}{19}$**

prompt: When Johan added the factors of 40 he left one out by mistake and thus arrived at a total of 70. The factor he left out was

solutions.title: Sum of divisors
solutions.body:
The factors of $40$ are $1,2,4,5,8,10,20,40$ with sum $90$. Since he got $70$, he left out $90-70=20$.

**Answer: (E) 20**

prompt: The diagram shows part of some scaffolding which consists of many equal rods joined together by connectors. The diagram shows a structure of length 2 units. The number of rods required to make a structure of length 40 units is

solutions.title: Count per block
solutions.body:
A structure of length $1$ is a box with $12$ rods. Each extra unit of length adds a new box sharing one face (4 rods) with the previous one, so it needs $12-4=8$ more rods. Length $n$ needs $12+8(n-1)=8n+4$ rods; for $n=40$: $324$. (Check: length $2$ gives $20$ rods.)

**Answer: (A) 324**

prompt: When $20^{11}$ is calculated, the number of digits in the result is

solutions.title: Split the power
solutions.body:
$20^{11}=2^{11}\cdot10^{11}=2048\cdot10^{11}=2.048\times10^{14}$. The number $2048$ has $4$ digits, followed by $11$ zeros: $15$ digits.

**Answer: (E) 15**

prompt: Rebecca has some money. She gives 10% of it to her sister, and then 20% of what is left to her brother. The percentage of the money that she kept for herself is

solutions.title: Multiply the remaining fractions
solutions.body:
After the first gift she has $90\%$; after the second she keeps $80\%$ of that: $0.9\times0.8=0.72=72\%$.

**Answer: (B) 72**

prompt: The formula for converting $^\circ$F into $^\circ$C is $C=\frac59(F-32)$. The temperature in $^\circ$C which is twice as big when converted to $^\circ$F is

solutions.title: Check
solutions.body:
$160^\circ$C $=\frac95\cdot160+32=288+32=320^\circ$F, which is twice $160$. ✓

**Answer: (E) 160°**

prompt: Boris is 4 km West of a fixed point $O$, travelling towards $O$ at a steady speed of 10 km per hour. Otto is 8 km East of $O$, travelling away from $O$ at a steady speed of 6 km per hour. When Boris reaches $O$, the distance of Otto from $O$ will be

solutions.title: Time then distance
solutions.body:
Boris needs $\frac4{10}=0.4$ h. In that time Otto travels $6\cdot0.4=2.4$ km further away, so he is $8+2.4=10.4$ km from $O$.

**Answer: (D) 10,4 km**

prompt: The diagram shows a triangular area that has been covered using identical square tiles of size 1 unit. If the triangle has sides of length 3 units and 6 units, and if each square tile can be cut at most once, then the minimum number of tiles needed to cover this triangle is

solutions.title: Whole tiles and cut tiles
solutions.body:
Put the right angle at the origin, legs $6$ (horizontal) and $3$ (vertical); the hypotenuse passes through the lattice points $(0,3),(2,2),(4,1),(6,0)$. Tiles lying completely inside the triangle: $4$ in the bottom row and $2$ in the middle row, so $6$ whole tiles. The remaining area $9-6=3$ consists of three right triangles with legs $2$ and $1$ along the hypotenuse, each of area $1$. Each such triangle spans two columns: it is a trapezoid piece in one tile together with a small triangle (legs $1$ and $\frac12$) in the next. Cutting one tile gives the trapezoid and a small triangle congruent to the piece needed in the neighbouring column, so one cut tile supplies a whole triangle of area $1$. Hence $3$ cut tiles are needed, and at least $6+3=9$ tiles in all.

**Answer: (C) 9**

prompt: The value of $1\frac12\times1\frac13\times1\frac14\times\dots\times1\frac1{19}$ is

solutions.title: Telescoping product
solutions.body:
$1\frac1k=\frac{k+1}{k}$, so the product is $\frac32\cdot\frac43\cdot\frac54\cdots\frac{20}{19}=\frac{20}{2}=10$.

**Answer: (B) 10**

prompt: The area of $\triangle ADP$ is $\frac15$ of the area of the rectangle. The proportion of the rectangle that is shaded is

solutions.title: Use triangle APB
solutions.body:
Triangle $APB$ has base $AB$ (a side of the rectangle) and apex $P$ on the opposite side, so it is half the rectangle. Hence $\triangle ADP+\triangle PBC=\frac12$ of the rectangle, and the shaded triangle $PBC$ is $\frac12-\frac15=\frac3{10}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac3{10}$**

prompt: Four different natural numbers all leave a remainder of 6 when divided by 7. If no two of them have a common factor, what is the least possible value of their sum?

solutions.title: Search the sequence
solutions.body:
The numbers come from $6,13,20,27,34,41,48,55,\dots$. If $6$ is used, the others must be odd and not multiples of $3$: $13,41,55,\dots$, giving at least $6+13+41+55=115$. Without $6$: $20$ and $34$ share a factor $2$, so among $13,20,27,34,41$ we can use at most one of them: the best is $13,20,27,41$ with sum $101$ (all pairs coprime: $20=2^2\cdot5$, $27=3^3$, $13$ and $41$ prime). Any other choice (e.g. $13,27,34,41$ or using $48$ or more) gives a larger sum.

**Answer: (B) 101**

prompt: A leap year has 366 consecutive days. What is the probability that a leap year has 53 Sundays in it?

solutions.title: Weeks and leftover days
solutions.body:
$366=52\cdot7+2$, so every weekday occurs $52$ times and exactly two weekdays (those of the first two days of the year) occur $53$ times. Sunday is one of them with probability $\frac27$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac27$**

prompt: Avril has cards: whenever an even number is on one side of the card, there must be an odd number on the other side. Six of her cards lie on a table, and four of those show an odd number. What is the maximum number of odd numbers we might see if we were able to look at both sides of each of those six cards?

solutions.title: Maximise the hidden odds
solutions.body:
The two cards showing an even number must have an odd number on the back: $2$ odd numbers. The four cards showing an odd number can have anything on the back, so up to $4$ more odd numbers. The total is $4$ (visible) $+2+4=10$.

**Answer: (D) 10**

prompt: A square piece of paper has squares cut off its corners. The sides of the removed squares have lengths 1 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm. Because of this the area of the piece of paper has been halved. The perimeter of the remaining piece of paper is

solutions.title: Original side and perimeter
solutions.body:
The removed area is $1+4+9+36=50$ cm$^2$, which is half the original, so the original square has area $100$ and side $10$ cm. Cutting a square from a corner replaces two edges by two edges of the same total length, so the perimeter does not change: $4\cdot10=40$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 40 cm**

prompt: Among the pupils at a school, the ratio of boys to girls is 2 : 3. If 5 more boys joined the school that ratio would become 7 : 10. The number of girls in the school is

solutions.title: Equation
solutions.body:
Let there be $2a$ boys and $3a$ girls. Then $\frac{2a+5}{3a}=\frac7{10}$, so $20a+50=21a$, $a=50$, and there are $3a=150$ girls.

**Answer: (E) 150**

prompt: When two circles of radius 2 cm each pass through the centre of the other, the distance in cm between the points of intersection $A$ and $B$ is

solutions.title: Equilateral triangle
solutions.body:
Let the centres be $O_1,O_2$. Then $O_1O_2=2$ and $O_1A=O_2A=2$, so $\triangle O_1O_2A$ is equilateral with side $2$. The line $AB$ is perpendicular to $O_1O_2$ and bisects it, so half of $AB$ is the height of this triangle, $\sqrt{2^2-1^2}=\sqrt3$. Hence $AB=2\sqrt3$.

**Answer: (D) $2\sqrt3$**

prompt: The figure shows a square with semicircles drawn on its sides. The length of a side of the square is 2 units. The area of the four-leaf shaded region is

solutions.title: Overlap of semicircles and square
solutions.body:
The four semicircles (radius $1$, drawn inwards) together have area $4\cdot\frac12\pi=2\pi$. They cover the whole square (area $4$) and the leaves are exactly the places where they overlap, so the leaf area is $2\pi-4$.

**Answer: (B) $2\pi-4$**

solutions.title: One leaf at a time
solutions.body:
Take the semicircles on two adjacent sides, centred at the midpoints $M_1$, $M_2$. Both circles pass through the centre $O$ of the square and the common corner $C$, and $\angle OM_1C=90^\circ$. The overlap is two congruent circular segments, each a quarter circle of radius $1$ ($\frac\pi4$) minus a right triangle with legs $1$ ($\frac12$). One leaf is $2\left(\frac\pi4-\frac12\right)=\frac\pi2-1$, and four leaves give $2\pi-4$.

**Answer: (B) $2\pi-4$**

prompt: A three-digit number is written down; then the same digits are reversed to give a new three-digit number. The smaller of these numbers is subtracted from the larger. Which of the following might be the result?

solutions.title: Divisible by 99
solutions.body:
If the digits are $X,Y,Z$ then $(100X+10Y+Z)-(100Z+10Y+X)=99(X-Z)$. So the result is a multiple of $99$. Among the options only $198=2\cdot99$ is one ($729,189,459,759$ are not).

**Answer: (C) 198**

prompt: A rectangular sheet of paper has a square removed from one end. The remaining rectangle has a square removed from one end. The rectangle now remaining has perimeter $\frac38$ that of the original rectangle. The ratio of the shorter side of the original rectangle to its longer side is

solutions.title: Name the lengths
solutions.body:
Let the original rectangle be $W\times H$ with $H<W$. Removing a square of side $H$ leaves an $H\times s$ rectangle with $s=W-H$; removing a square of side $s$ leaves the final rectangle $s\times t$ with $t=H-s$. So $H=s+t$ and $W=H+s=2s+t$. The perimeter condition $2(s+t)=\frac38\cdot2(W+H)=\frac38\cdot2(3s+2t)$ gives $8(s+t)=3(3s+2t)$, i.e. $s=2t$. Then $H:W=(s+t):(2s+t)=3t:5t=3:5$.

**Answer: (A) 3 : 5**

solutions.title: Check
solutions.body:
Take $H=3$, $W=5$: remove a $3\times3$ square, leaving $3\times2$; remove a $2\times2$ square, leaving $2\times1$ with perimeter $6$. The original perimeter is $16$ and $\frac38\cdot16=6$. ✓

**Answer: (A) 3 : 5**

prompt: Three-digit numbers are formed that use only different odd digits (so not 551, for instance). The sum of all the possible numbers is

solutions.title: Each digit equally often
solutions.body:
There are $5\cdot4\cdot3=60$ such numbers. In each position, each of $1,3,5,7,9$ appears equally often, namely $\frac{60}{5}=12$ times, so the digits in each column add to $12\cdot25=300$. The total is $300\cdot100+300\cdot10+300=33\,300$.

**Answer: (B) 33 300**
